Over a prolific career, the report states that Skerritt established himself through a series of definitive supporting and leading performances. On the big screen, he famously portrayed **Captain Dallas** in the sci-fi horror classic *Alien*, bringing a grounded gravity to the doomed spaceship commander. Film audiences also know him from the military blockbuster *Top Gun*, where he took on the role of **Viper**. Transitioning successfully to the television medium, the actor later stepped into the shoes of a small-town lawman, starring as the sheriff in the acclaimed television series *Picket Fences*. 

## Industry Impact and Cultural Context

Character actors of Skerritt's caliber often form the structural backbone of Hollywood storytelling, bridging the gap between major box office draws and grounded dramatic realism. Throughout his career, performers like Skerritt provided the steady institutional counterweights—whether commanding a star freighter or presiding over a quirky municipal court—that allowed high-concept narratives to maintain emotional resonance.

articles.title: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia
articles.summary: Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.
articles.content: Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.
articles.aiArticle:
The era of a popular alternative web navigator is drawing to a close. According to TechCrunch, The Browser Company has announced that the **Arc** browser will officially sunset on **December 22, 2026**. 

## The Pivot to Dia

The decision to shutter the product stems from a strategic shift within the company. TechCrunch reports that the organization is now pivoting its resources toward developing **Dia**, its newer product offering. While Arc cultivated a fiercely loyal following among dedicated enthusiasts, the report notes that it ultimately failed to achieve the mass-market adoption needed to genuinely rival dominant platforms like Google Chrome, which has historically dominated desktop browsing shares much like legacy software systems that once required extensive [PHP web development](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/php-the-three-little-letters-wreaking-havoc-across-the-web) to build the early internet.

## Why This Matters

This transition underscores the brutal economic realities of challenging entrenched tech monopolies. For everyday users and power-users alike, the loss of Arc means bidding farewell to a radical interface that attempted to rethink how humans interact with tabs, workspaces, and web applications. Cultivating a passionate niche community is rarely enough to sustain a venture-backed software project if user acquisition stalls before reaching mainstream ubiquity—a harsh lesson familiar to founders navigating difficult markets, similar to how [early-stage startup founders secure Series A funding](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/investors-break-down-how-founders-can-raise-a-series-a-today) by proving massive scalability rather than just high user satisfaction. 

## What to Watch

Observers and former power-users will be closely monitoring how gracefully the transition is handled ahead of the December deadline. Key questions remain regarding data migration paths for existing Arc loyalists and whether Dia can successfully capture the mainstream audience that eluded its predecessor.

Sources: [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/22/arc-browser-sunsets-december-22-as-the-browser-company-doubles-down-on-dia/)

articles.title: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing
articles.summary: Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing. The plans, put…
articles.content: Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing. The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks. Continue reading...
articles.aiArticle:
British authorities are preparing to scale back post-2008 regulatory measures that were originally established to ensure senior financial executives face accountability for corporate misconduct, according to **Business | The Guardian**. The proposed adjustments aim to eliminate what regulators describe as redundant administrative obstacles for financial institutions operating within the country's major banking hub.

## Overhauling Post-Crisis Accountability

The upcoming policy shifts are projected by regulators to generate approximately **£2bn** in savings for businesses across a ten-year timeframe, the report states. These regulations trace their origins back to the severe economic downturn of **2008**, a period when policymakers introduced rigorous standards to penalize institutional leadership for severe failures. By dismantling these oversight mechanisms, proponents argue that firms will operate with greater efficiency, though critics warn the changes could diminish the personal liability traditionally placed on corporate directors. Similar cost-cutting measures and structural shifts continue to sweep through the sector, as seen elsewhere when financial institutions announce comprehensive workforce reductions amid [Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/barclays-to-cut-jobs-as-bank-s-bosses-hail-ai-productivity-advances).

## Differing Perspectives on Deregulation

Proponents of the rollback maintain that streamlining compliance requirements will maintain competitiveness for the UK financial sector. According to the reporting, authorities emphasize that removing these specific obligations is a necessary step to foster economic growth and reduce red tape. Conversely, consumer advocates and governance watchdogs contend that weakening these post-crisis safeguards risks returning the banking industry to the unchecked practices that preceded the global financial collapse. 

*Context:* Following the global financial crisis of 2007-2008, governments worldwide instituted sweeping statutory frameworks to curb reckless banking behavior and restore public trust in capital markets. The UK's Senior Managers and Certification Regime, established in the wake of those events, sought to prevent executives from evading responsibility by clearly assigning liability for specific operational areas.

*Why this matters:* The stakes center on the balance between national economic competitiveness and financial stability. If oversight is loosened too significantly, ordinary taxpayers and consumers may absorb the financial impact of future corporate failures. Conversely, proponents argue that overly strict compliance regimes stifle innovation and drive capital away from domestic markets.

*What to watch:* Observers will monitor upcoming parliamentary debates and formal responses from consumer protection organizations as the regulatory amendments move closer to implementation. Further announcements from watchdogs regarding specific rule exemptions will clarify the full scope of the deregulation agenda.

Sources: [Business | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/22/uk-relax-post-2008-rules-hold-city-bosses-accountable-wrongdoing)

Founders navigating their initial phase should look beyond immediate customer acquisition to build lasting commercial momentum, according to insights shared at the Disrupt conference. Luke Arno, who leads Go-To-Market efforts at Lovable, joined Ben Broca of Polska and Tomasz Tunguz from Theory Ventures to outline best practices for new ventures during their opening months. Rather than chasing short-term billing targets, the panel advised early-stage builders to focus on foundational positioning. This guidance arrives as many emerging companies struggle to balance product development with commercial demands during their formative quarter.

As startup accelerators and events like the [TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 Startup Battlefield 200](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/techcrunch-disrupt-startup-battlefield-celebrating-outstanding-achievements) highlight innovative achievements across the sector, leadership teams face mounting pressure to demonstrate rapid traction. 

## Understanding the Long-Term Commercial Stakes

This debate over early commercial strategy cuts to the core of how venture-backed companies allocate scarce capital and engineering hours. When founders prioritize volume over product alignment, teams often burn through runway satisfying mismatched clients who demand bespoke features rather than a scalable core platform. Conversely, ignoring early market feedback entirely risks building in a vacuum. For investors and operators alike, striking the right balance determines whether a young enterprise secures subsequent funding rounds or stalls out before finding product-market fit.

## What to Watch

Observers should monitor whether venture firms adjust their seed-stage evaluation metrics away from raw monthly recurring revenue toward retention and product usage indicators. Future conference panels and accelerator cohorts will likely reflect these shifting priorities as market conditions evolve.

## The Shift in Allegiance

The report states that what began as policy disagreements has transformed into explicit identity-based attacks from the political right. According to The Verge, young Indian Americans who previously aligned with conservative platforms report feeling alienated by xenophobic tropes circulating among high-profile figures and online commentators. The publication highlights that figures like **Vivek Ramaswamy** have faced racially charged scrutiny during campaign cycles, illustrating a broader pattern where South Asian candidates and citizens are subjected to coded or overt bigotry from within conservative circles.

Historically, immigrant communities have found common ground with conservative values centered on economic mobility, entrepreneurship, and traditional family structures. However, the report indicates that the mainstreaming of nationalist rhetoric is fraying these political alliances. As political parties aggressively court every demographic slice in competitive regions, the alienation of a fast-growing, economically influential electorate carries significant electoral consequences. For decades, minority outreach has been a central calculation in American politics; when a major party permits or ignores identity-based vitriol, it risks forfeiting a generation of upwardly mobile voters. articles.aiArticle:
Google has issued an urgent advisory urging Android device owners to apply a software update immediately, following legislative shifts in Canada that have altered how certain regions handle seasonal clock changes. According to a report by **The Verge**, the warning arrives as several Canadian jurisdictions move to adopt permanent daylight saving time, exposing a vulnerability in how older mobile operating systems calculate local hours. While policymakers push for year-round evening sunlight, the underlying technical infrastructure of everyday pocket devices is struggling to keep pace with these legislative updates.

## Technical Glitches Threaten Smartphone Clocks

The root of the issue lies in outdated time zone databases embedded within mobile software, which dictate when clocks should spring forward or fall back. Without the newly released patches, affected smartphones risk displaying incorrect times, throwing off morning alarms, calendar appointments, and automated system backups. **The Verge** notes that while major technology companies frequently issue routine patches for timezone adjustments, abrupt or fragmented regional policy changes create severe logistical hurdles for automated system updates. 

This technical hiccup in North America echoes broader challenges in software stability, reminiscent of how developers routinely scramble to patch vulnerabilities across complex codebases, similar to the widespread anxiety caused when critical platforms face sudden security crises like the recent [PHP armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/php-armageddon-openai-google-s-wiz-find-ancient-holes-panicking-the-internet). Mobile operating systems rely heavily on absolute precision, meaning even minor legislative alterations to regional timekeeping can trigger cascading software failures if device internal clocks drift out of sync with official atomic time servers.

## Why This Matters

As governments increasingly tinker with historical timekeeping frameworks, the stakes for everyday consumers and global enterprise systems grow exponentially. When regional legislation clashes with fixed software logic, millions of users face immediate disruptions in their daily routines, ranging from missed flights to failed digital authentications that rely on precise time stamps. 

Historically, daylight saving time was enacted during World War I to conserve energy by extending evening daylight, yet modern society's absolute dependence on synchronized digital infrastructure means that altering these rhythms now creates disproportionate friction. For everyday citizens, a simple hour discrepancy can derail work schedules and transportation logistics, while businesses face potential synchronization errors in database logs and financial transactions.

## What to Watch

Industry observers should monitor whether other federal and state legislatures follow Canada’s lead in permanently altering seasonal time laws, which would force smartphone manufacturers to continually overhaul their default time zone libraries. Analysts will also track how effectively major tech firms push over-the-air patches to legacy hardware that no longer receives active OS support, as unpatched devices remain uniquely vulnerable to perpetual time drift.

articles.content: Despite being announced just a few weeks ago , both Amazon and Best Buy are now offering the latest Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K for 50 percent off, bringing the price down to an all-time low of $29.99. The most notable new feature is that the Fire TV Stick 4K no longer requires a separate power connection, meaning it can draw all the juice it needs from the USB port on your TV. It supports 4K at up to 60fps, with HDR10 Plus for higher contrast, although it’s worth noting that it doesn’t allow for side-loading apps like some older models. Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K (2026) Where to Buy: $59.99 $29.99 at Amazon $59.99 $29.99 at Best Buy Amazon updated the Fire TV OS earlier this year with a redesigned UI, closer Alexa Plus integration, and various improvements to the mobile app, all of which are supported on the new hardware. You’ll also get a revamped remote, which features a new asymmetrical design with a rounded bottom and buttons with a more tactile feel. For connectivity, the Fire TV Stick 4K has Bluetooth 5.3 and Wi-Fi 6.

articles.content: A lot of people are snagging a PlayStation 5 ahead of Grand Theft Auto VI ’s November 19th launch. You could pay full price at one of many retailers, but why do that when you can save $100 on a Sony-refurbished console that has the same one-year warranty? It’s a great time to consider one because company has a new limited-time bundle. Through this page , you can select either a refurbished digital or disc-based console for $499 or $549, respectively, and add a refurbished DualSense to your order that’s $40 off its usual price. For instance, a white DualSense tacks just $18 to your total, while one of the fancier colors, like sterling silver, adds $23. It’s an affordable way to stock up to cover a two-player household. The refurbished controller also includes a one-year warranty. Sony PlayStation 5 slim (refurbished) Where to Buy: $558 $518 at Sony (digital, with refurb DualSense) $608 $568 at Sony (disc, with refurb DualSense) One thing to note about the refurbished consoles is that they include a 1TB SSD. Sony’s digital edition console at stores is currently equipped with 825GB of built-in storage (the disc edition still has 1TB), so it’s nice that this version includes a little extra space for games. Like all PlayStation 5 consoles, these support PCIe 4.0 M.2 SSDs equipped with heatsinks for extra storage, though like RAM, those are pretty pricey at the moment.

Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of the capital of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. articles.content: Protecting jobs and strengthening energy security in the short term does not mean wavering on Labour’s deep commitment to a cleaner, greener future Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval On Wednesday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, gave the go-ahead for gas production to begin at the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. This has been the subject of fierce debate for many years, with strong views on both sides. I want to explain what the decision means and how it fits with Britain’s climate commitments. At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter. In the longer term, it will significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK’s energy supply for more than a decade. Wednesday’s decision will also protect hundreds of jobs in Scotland and add almost £3bn to the UK economy over the lifetime of the project. As tennis circuits span the globe in search of emerging talent, a unique dual-heritage prospect is quietly making waves on the international stage by competing under the French flag despite his strong English lineage. According to **BBC Sport**, rising player **Felix Balshaw** has been steadily advancing through the world tennis rankings while carving out an athletic identity distinct from his family's famous rugby roots. 

## A Sporting Dynasty Crossing Borders

The young athlete carries a notable pedigree into his professional tennis career, being the son of an **English Rugby World Cup winner**, as detailed by the report. While many children of elite athletes naturally gravitate toward their parents' specific disciplines—frequently drawing comparisons to international sporting upheavals such as the dramatic moments seen when [England face exit](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/mcdermott-blames-rugby-league-world-cup-format-as-england-face-exit) in other global tournaments—**Balshaw** chose the individual intensity of the tennis court over the team dynamics of rugby. His choice to represent France marks an intriguing cross-channel dynamic, blending English rugby history with French tennis development structures.

Tennis is an unforgiving individual sport where financial sustainability, mental resilience, and geographic federation support often dictate whether a promising junior successfully transitions to the senior ATP tour. For a dual-national competitor like **Balshaw**, navigating these early career stages requires balancing national federation backing with the immense pressure of living up to a celebrated athletic surname. Similar administrative complexities and high-stakes appointments frequently shape major sporting trajectories, much like leadership transitions seen in events overseen by figures with diverse racquet-sport backgrounds, exemplified by industry appointments such as an [ex-tennis pro Megan Rose appointed to lead 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup in US](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/ex-tennis-pro-megan-rose-appointed-to-lead-men-s-rugby-world).

articles.aiArticle:
Websites globally are facing a massive wave of security threats as malicious actors launch millions of automated attempts to exploit a severe vulnerability in the PHP programming language, according to **Business | The Guardian**. The high-volume attacks have forced both corporate networks and government entities to take drastic action, including pulling web portals offline entirely to install urgent security patches.

PHP serves as the digital foundation for a vast majority of the internet, powering approximately **70%** of all sites online. Because of this widespread ubiquity, the sudden discovery of a critical code flaw has triggered an unprecedented scramble among system administrators. As digital defenses race against automated exploit tools, understanding the technical nature of this emergency is vital, leading many to examine [what PHP is and how bad the computer language flaw is](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/what-is-php-and-how-bad-is-the-computer-language-flaw-causing) as organizations struggle to contain the fallout.

## Global Fallout and Mitigation Efforts

According to the report, the scale of the incident has caught many digital infrastructure teams off guard. Rather than risking data breaches or system takeovers, numerous enterprise operators and public sector agencies chose to disconnect their servers from the public internet entirely. This emergency downtime aims to give engineers a secure window to apply necessary software updates and verify system integrity. 

The widespread disruption highlights vulnerabilities in foundational web technologies that millions of businesses rely on daily. For a deeper look at how this crisis unfolded across international borders, readers can consult our previous reporting on the [flaw in the PHP computer language that led to global website shutdowns](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/flaw-in-php-computer-language-leads-to-shutdown-of-websites-around-world). Security analysts continue to monitor server logs as organizations try to determine the full extent of the attempted intrusions.

## Analysis: Why This Matters and What Lies Ahead

*(Context: This section provides analytical depth regarding the broader implications of the security event.)*

The current crisis underscores the fragile nature of modern digital infrastructure, where a single coding flaw in an open-source language can jeopardize a significant portion of the global web. When core components like PHP are compromised, the stakes extend far beyond temporary downtime, threatening sensitive user data, e-commerce transactions, and essential public services. Small and medium enterprises, which often lack dedicated round-the-clock cybersecurity teams, remain especially vulnerable to prolonged outages and potential data exfiltration.

*(What to watch: Observers should monitor whether patch adoption rates outpace the spread of automated malware scanners. Regulators may also face renewed pressure to mandate stricter security baselines for open-source dependencies used in critical public infrastructure.)*

articles.content: Bruno Fernandes will remain as Manchester United captain and will not be disciplined for his post-match criticism of Michael Carrick after the 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.
articles.aiArticle:
Manchester United midfielder **Bruno Fernandes** will keep the club captaincy and avoid any internal disciplinary action following his public critique of coaching staff, according to BBC Sport. The decision comes in the wake of a heavy **4-1** defeat to Como in the Champions League, a result that intensified pressure surrounding the Old Trafford dugout. 

## The Aftermath of European Humiliation

The fallout from the continental setback centered largely on post-match remarks delivered by the Portuguese playmaker. Following the humbling loss, Fernandes voiced sharp frustration regarding the team's tactical setup under **Michael Carrick**. Rather than punishing the skipper for airing grievances in public, club hierarchy opted to maintain stability by keeping the armband firmly in his possession. 

This retention of leadership status arrives amid mounting scrutiny over squad performance and on-field organization. Readers seeking a deeper look into the tactical issues can review our analysis on [breaking down Man Utd's tactics after Fernandes' criticism](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/breaking-down-man-utd-s-tactics-after-fernandes-criticism). Tensions behind the scenes have reportedly run high, with previous reports highlighting an [‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tactics](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/angry-carrick-on-the-brink-as-fernandes-hits-out-at-manchester-united). 

## Broader Context and Stakes

Manchester United has long operated under intense media scrutiny, where every post-match comment from a senior player is magnified by global audiences and supporters alike. When star players publicly question tactical approaches, it often signals a deeper disconnect between the dressing room and the technical staff, placing immense pressure on club executives to manage internal harmony while results falter on the pitch.

Management must now balance player accountability with the immediate need to arrest a slide in form, especially during high-stakes European campaigns where squad unity is paramount. Failure to mend potential rifts between leadership figures and the coaching staff risks alienating supporters and derailing the remainder of the season.

## What to Watch

articles.title: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning | Leander Schaerlaeckens
articles.summary: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer Sign up for our free newsletter here Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner.…
articles.content: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer Sign up for our free newsletter here Poor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa president Gianni Infantino dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along. Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets . Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University. articles.title: PHP: The three little letters wreaking havoc across the web
articles.summary: Two vulnerabilities found in the programming language PHP put enormous swaths of the internet in danger . By some accounts, up to 70 percent of websites use PHP in some capacity. It powers Wikipedia, WordPress, Drupal, and a host of other popular sites and…
articles.content: Two vulnerabilities found in the programming language PHP put enormous swaths of the internet in danger . By some accounts, up to 70 percent of websites use PHP in some capacity. It powers Wikipedia, WordPress, Drupal, and a host of other popular sites and platforms, including DeviantArt and 4Chan, which were temporarily shut down after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Even governments weren’t immune. But it’s not as simple as updating a few servers. The vulnerability exists in every version of PHP dating back roughly 20 years, many of which are no longer supported. That means some older sites and services that are no longer actively maintained are at risk, leaving them with little option but to permanently shut down. Here’s all the latest developments in what security firm Wiz has called “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered … in software history.” The Internet Archive was briefly forced offline because of PHP. Two old-school Japanese mobile games are shutting down over the PHP exploit. The PHP2Shell exploit hit Cloudflare hard. articles.content: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs For months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee . In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official : Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival. Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure . The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer , Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice). articles.title: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game
articles.summary: (Roundhouse, London) With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse It’s 20 years since Amy Winehouse released her masterpiece Back to Black and 15…
articles.content: (Roundhouse, London) With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse It’s 20 years since Amy Winehouse released her masterpiece Back to Black and 15 since she died at a frighteningly young age. A good way to appreciate how special she was is to watch the Amy Winehouse Band trot through a few lesser songs and cover versions and spot what’s missing: her playfulness, bite, anarchic charisma and taste. Winehouse mixed soul, jazz, hip-hop, two-tone and 60s girl groups because she loved that music more than anything. Without her animating fandom, a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals is just a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals; for all her old band’s precision and gusto, it has no pressing reason to exist. The main event, in which Back to Black producers including Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi hand-pick singers such as Jorja Smith, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae to recreate the album, is stronger except that it’s primarily staged for a BBC TV show, which means the flow is broken by onstage interviews and hagiographical patter from Jo Whiley. It’s a little grating to be constantly told that a concert is amazing even as it unfolds, but that’s TV for you. Continue reading...

articles.title: Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’
articles.summary: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine…
articles.content: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford? TopTramp That’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people. Your Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown. You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends. I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00s Zach Braff would make it in the present day the way you did? KamesJ Back then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky. Continue reading...

The Australian author used only about 25 lines from Jane Austen’s first published novel for her screenplay, inventing most of the dialogue herself. To be able to mimic that very distinctive voice, Reid had to dive headfirst into studying Austen’s rhythm and sentence structure. “I got so immersed in the language it infected my own speech. I would be describing someone I just met, and I’d be like, ‘Oh, he was most amiable!’” Reid says, laughing. “It was a kind of insanity.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Bill Gates says to prepare for 20 years of ‘tumultuous’ AI disruption
articles.summary: Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation. You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late…
articles.content: Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation. You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late August titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical.” In his piece, Gates ratcheted up his rhetoric around AI safety, writing that “even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history.” In interviews since , Gates has called AI “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near,” and that AI “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing.” It is clear he does not think the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated efforts from the AI industry itself, is sufficient to combat this threat. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . So I wanted to know: Is Bill Gates an AI doomer? I also had a series of questions downstream from what he’s been arguing about AI. How can we ever hope to control AI, and align it to humanity, if we can’t even agree on what it is and whether it’s conscious ? How would you even technically construct a solution to alignment that could be enforced, not just for closed-source models but open-source ones, too? Bill gave us a big chunk of his time to dig into these issues with him, and the resulting conversation is a really illuminating one. He thinks we need to prepare for roughly two decades of AI disruption, and he says this period could be so painful it might split society in two — between people comfortable living near the technological frontier, and those who reject it. We also talked about the labor considerations, the nihilism of younger generations toward technological progress, and what should make us hopeful about the future. This is a deep one. Okay: Bill Gates, the cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Bill Gates, you are the co-founder and former CEO of Microsoft. You’re also the chairman of the Gates Foundation. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. It’s good to talk to you again. You and I have spoken many times over the years. I would say that the circumstances of this conversation feel very different. Previously, when you and I would talk, you were always very hopeful about technology and what it could bring. You had a Netflix series a few years ago. You talked to The Verge , and I want to just read you this quote. You said, “I believe AI is a beneficial thing, we just need to shape it in the right way.” I would say you still agree with that, you just think the time to shape it is now. Yeah, I agree with that. I’d say the response broadly hasn’t been adequate to the speed that the challenge is arising. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way I want to have this conversation with you in three parts. I want to understand how you feel about AI as a technology today and why it’s advancing so quickly. I’m very curious about the technology, and the technical solutions to potentially control it. There are policy solutions as well, but it seems like we have to build an awful lot of technology. I’m also very curious to talk about who might impose those solutions and controls, because that seems very much up for debate right now as well. So let’s just start at the start. What has made you feel the urgency that AI is arriving at a speed that means we’re not ready to control it? The progress over the last year has been really quite amazing, starting with the ability to write code and find cyber flaws, the ability to reason in biology, the ability to form relationships with kids or other people, the ability to disrupt the job market. The incredible power that exists today means that every one of those things will happen and society needs to be ready. Do you see that happening as a technology as a whole or in the products that are instantiated by the companies that are making AI today? What I mean is that AI is a broad set of models that exist in the world, some open source, some proprietary. Then there are the companies that make these products and there are the leaders of those companies that make these products. At every level, there’s a different relationship you or I might have to AI. Are you seeing these risks and these capabilities broadly in the field, or in the particular companies led by the particular people? The risk isn’t one model versus another model. Certainly, the near-term danger of models where you can remove all the safeguards is very high and quite different from models where you monitor to make sure that cyberattackers and bioterrorists are not able to exploit the capability of the model to do gigantic harm. The big near-term risk really comes from models without safeguards. On a longer timeframe, the control issue relates to any state-of-the-art model, but it’s always easier when you can make sure safeguards are maintained. The reason I’m asking that question that way is maybe you don’t trust Sam Altman today, but you trust Dario Amodei. Or maybe you don’t trust either one of those and you trust Satya Nadella at Microsoft, and that is a market dynamic where maybe we’re all going to pick the safest model or the safest company, and you think that is diffuse. You think eventually the technology will just get to a place where it’s harmful or can cause these harms because it exists? For somebody doing a cyberattack with the model, it’s not about choosing a model. It doesn’t matter what model you choose. If Anthropic has safeguards in place, maybe it can’t. This is their approach currently. I’m just pushing on that. Yes, certainly the models where they make sure the safeguards are not removed and they’re putting a lot of effort in seeing how those models are being used, monitoring the activity, the near-term risk from those models is not gigantic. It’s more where somebody can remove all the safeguards where the cyberattacks are available today. When you say cyberattacks, is it the things like the Hugging Face breach and the other cybersecurity incidents we’ve seen out of the labs that have made you feel that thresholds have been crossed, and you need to speak up more about the controls that are needed? It’s the basic power of the models towards everything: social relationships, the job market, cyberattacks, bioterrorism attacks. We’ve crossed the threshold of capability that this is by far the most dangerous technology ever invented, and it’ll have pervasive effects in the economy and how war is fought. The industry is actually speaking up about that quite a bit, but the awareness or even the willingness to believe these things about, “This time is different,” once you get outside the industry, it’s very, very low. People are often looking at the past and saying, “All the fears about technology in terms of its disruption, including to the job market, never were borne out. So this must be another example just like those. These people who are warning of all these different problems must just be wrong and we can ignore them.” Some outsiders say, “Get better PR companies.” But that ignores the fact that these warnings are the truth We see this with our audience as well, right? “We can’t release the model, it’s too dangerous.” “This is just hype to prop up the bubble.” And on and on we go. Yeah. None of the warnings being made about these models by industry insiders are at all insincere. They’re absolutely the truth and it’s pretty much universal. You can even go back to the founding story of OpenAI designed to say, “If we get too powerful, maybe we can not open Pandora’s box,” or to DeepMind’s negotiation with Google management. The people close to this are very concerned about misuse, job impacts, social relationship impacts, and I’d say it’s impressive to have an industry that’s speaking out as vividly as they are. Some outsiders say, “Get better PR companies.” But that ignores the fact that these warnings are the truth. You’ve obviously moved back and forth in your life between commercializing software and technology and being a humanitarian. There’s something about these companies in particular where they all started with very high-minded ideals — all three of them, Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepMind — to build AGI. Some of the things, like cyberattacks and the job market thing, even in the next two to three years, you’ll see significant negative effects in those two areas Do you think that that is enough to overcome people’s skepticism or fear of the AI models they encounter today? Because that is very much how the companies think about it. No, come on. I think it’s unfair to say they were totally on a doomer message and now they’ve switched to some other message. These two things are deeply entangled. AI will eventually be able to model human biology in such a way that you’ll understand the side effects of a drug without having to do human trials. We’re not there, but in the next five to 10 years, there’s a very good chance these in silico models will give us that capability. Biology is very complex, AI is extremely good given enough data, and there are new tools to gather and feed it more data. It’s very, very good at dealing with complex systems, so it’s almost perfect for biology. But no, that doesn’t mean that people will feel good about the downsides. How quickly do the good things arrive? How quickly do you look at your medical bill and go, “Wow, that’s really low”? Or you say, “I want to buy a new house, wow, these houses are sure cheap”? The good stuff does take time. Some of the things, like cyberattacks and the job market thing, even in the next two to three years, you’ll see significant negative effects in those two areas. You have a number of ideas for how you would stop those negative effects, or prevent or at least mitigate them, in your letter. Moderate them, yes. Ameliorate might be the right word. Yes, exactly. And they’re not small. You have a quote here that says, “We need a response far greater than the United States national security response in the wake of 9/11.” You want to set up an international body that somehow makes everyone do the right thing. These are challenging ideas. Absolutely. When we blew off nuclear bombs in World War II, did we expect that we’d go 80 more years without that happening? I’d give us a good grade on that. Things like caring for poor countries and helping them out — although right now we’re not prioritizing that as much as I think we should or we did in the past, we’ve done a very good job on that. This will be a greater challenge than anything humanity’s ever achieved. One of the things that strikes me about the comparison to nuclear, which has come up quite a bit on Decoder recently , is the government built the nuclear weapons. Sure, they had some contractors, but these were government projects and eventually the technology was in control of the government, and we never let regular people have it. Think about Muse in the context of nuclear weapons. Do you think it’s a mistake to have consumer agentic AI products like Muse and Dots that might not have the controls? Muse happens to be powered by Meta’s model, which is still a closed-source model. I do think allowing people through open weights to remove all safeguards is irresponsible in terms of the cyber and bio risk that comes from that. For these agents, there’ll be some early problems in terms of how they’re set up, but I fundamentally think people will have personal agents. Muse is a very nice step forward. I talked to Alexandr Wang about it, congratulated him, and even though it’ll have challenges, personal agents will help people get things done. Muse is the first truly great consumer AI product. One of the reasons people don’t like AI a lot in a diffuse way is they experience cheap free models and AI overviews or they use the free ChatGPT and it hallucinates and it lies to them, but Muse actually does things and it’s a good consumer product. But I wonder — in the nuclear age, we were not saying, “Everyone is going to have a nuclear reactor at home that we haven’t built the safety guards for.” There’s something here. The notion of letting everybody make smallpox at home or make nuclear weapons at home, of course, and you can parody some of these people saying, “Don’t worry about safeguards.” It’s taking that position. “We are not serious about the safety things.” But the personal agent thing is an expected development. AIs are really cool just as I intellectually explore things, even the work of the Gates Foundation. I’m far more empowered. But I agree with you, it’ll get out to more people in this personal agent form. The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd All the models we’ve been talking about right now effectively run on data centers owned by big companies. One of the arguments here is, “If they do something really wrong, you can just sue them and that will provide a deterrent or at least an incentive to create safety systems.” I’m not sure product liability is the way to go, but it has come up a lot that product liability itself will keep the industry in line. Then there’s the flip side, which is that you can just go buy a Mac Studio and run an open source and open weight model on it and it can do whatever you want. I’m not sure where any of that liability would lie or what would control or align the behaviors of those open source models. Do you think that that is an ever-growing risk? Do you think that that can be controlled? The notion that liability laws are how we’re going to manage AI safety will be looked back on as absurd. When bad people do bioattacks, you don’t go to the court and say, “Oh, okay.” Even for finding who is doing these attacks, the liability model fails in every respect because it’s not the AI companies themselves. It’s the people who take particularly the models without safeguards and do these things. We will take AI safety more seriously than we take airline safety, drug safety, and car safety. That is guaranteed. Whether it’s going to be enough… This is harder, harder than nuclear weapons, harder than any of those other domains. But what are you going to do about an open source model running on a PC that somebody built with just a random Nvidia graphics card in it? I would hope that with models above a certain capability, we find a way to require the safeguards and monitoring to be maintained in those models. I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see. But where do you impose the limit? A sovereign country says that models that are capable of sophisticated cyberattacks have to have safeguards kept in them. Sure. You can be open in the sense that you’re free, you can be open in the sense that you’re totally customizable, but you have to stay on platforms where, as you customize it, it’s checking to see if you’re customizing out the safeguards and monitoring and refusing to let you do that. So it means sovereigns go and say, “Are these trusted platforms able to perform this function or not?” I’m asking very nuts and bolts. Where would you technically implement that regulation? Through the laws of the United States. Sure, but you have to put them somewhere. Is it at the Hugging Face, which distributes some of these models? Is it at the chip level? No, it’s exactly what I said: Models above a certain capacity can only be run on platforms that certify that, as they’re customized, it’s not taking out the safeguards. I admit as time goes on that, if we don’t fairly soon decide to do that, you’re going to have a level of capability that’s out in dark corners that you won’t be able to see Just to pull this apart, maybe I’m not quite getting it — is the Mac Studio a platform in that case that would have to pay attention to what code it’s running? You would not let a model past a certain capability be copied down to a client machine unless you’d somehow figured out how to monitor down to that client machine, which is very doable. But in the near term, most of these really frontier models are going to run more on Hugging Face or you could have them on GitHub. You can have all sorts of people be in the business of providing the platforms that maintain safeguards. Just to get this right, it seems like you would enforce the regulation at the platform and distribution level and not so much at the chip level. Not at the chip level, no. Because it feels to me at some point even the cheap, free, open source models will be capable enough as the models we have today. That’s right. And then you will have a big problem. If those are open weights in such a way that all safeguards can be removed, then you’re going to have a very high level of cyberattacks and bioattacks. You can then say, “Okay, let’s rewrite all the code that we have today to be less subject to attack or let’s do biosurveillance in a very deep way,” which are things I believe we need to do in addition to these other restrictions. We’re proposing again a lot of new capabilities, right? Yeah. We’re going to impose some restrictions on GitHub. GitHub does not have a lot of restrictions on what code it can distribute today. It has some, but it doesn’t have this kind of set of restrictions. When you put a state-of-the-art model that’s capable of profound cyberattacks or bioattacks on GitHub, it would say, “I’ve gone to the U.S. government and certified that I don’t let people customize out the safeguards.” I do not think that we currently live in a time of high trust in institutions. It just doesn’t feel that way to me. In fact, mostly we’ve torn them down. Elon Musk showed up and he tore down USAID. I know you have strong feelings about that. That was a mistake. We have mostly torn down our institutions, for good and bad. No, that’s a little too strong. Our institutions- They’re weakened. They’re somewhat weakened, yeah. Somewhat weakened. It’s a very nice way of putting it. Trust in them is very low. We could probably do another full hour on AI drug discovery and whether a significant part of the population will trust the products of that work because they don’t trust pharma companies today. They don’t have to trust pharma companies today. They have to trust the FDA review process. I’m not sure they trust that either. Across the board, trust is low. Then they can walk away from taking them. When they get cancer, they can say, “No, I don’t want to take that cancer drug.” As far as I know, people do take drugs. It’s a thriving business and people take them because they have proven benefits. All I’m saying is, right now it feels like trust in institutions, particularly in America but around the world, is in decline. You are proposing a new class of institutions, potentially a new class of global institutions that might impose restrictions that are novel. At some point we need to say open source models, open weight models cannot do things and the government is going to reach into them and say whether or not they can do the things. No, they’ll make sure that the platforms don’t allow the safeguards to be taken away. How do you regain the institutional trust to impose these controls? Let’s say we don’t do this and we let models go off and do cyberattacks and bioattacks. Do you think that’s going to increase trust or human wellbeing? That’s the alternative. This is why I’m asking about it. This is why I asked about my kids and nihilism. I truly wonder about this. I’m not sure we’ll succeed at this, but I guarantee you this is doable. The FDA is very complex. The airline safety regulations are very complex. Now with AI, you can do an even better job with the same number of people in those organizations. It’s this weirdly recursive thing where AI will be involved in AI safety and auditing and a variety of things like that. Yes, this requires taking action, and I’m suggesting it’s only a matter of how bad the incidents are before we take action. People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices I can sense your urgency about the harms. I can also sense your enthusiasm about the benefits over the long term, but we’re sitting here talking about trust. We’re going to put this on YouTube. I know you know what some of the YouTube commenters are going to say. They’re going to say, “Why should we trust Bill Gates? He had a relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.” How do you respond to that? Is it that the urgency is over that, or do you have a more specific response? People shouldn’t take everything I do at face value. I have all sorts of mistakes that I’ve made, weaknesses that I have, biases I bring to these questions. They ought to just take what I’m saying and add it to the voices. I’ve been in the technology industry thinking about AI my whole life, writing software, thinking about the power of software. I admit I was very fascinated as AI started to finally make progress. It was actually pretty slow until recently. I’m amazed and it’s actually helping me do my job in some incredible ways. But yes, I’m just one voice, an imperfect voice. I doubt you’ll find a perfect voice, but people can judge it however they like. I would say voices people trust are in short supply. I agree with that. When you go and talk to the people in this industry, it’s a bunch of young CEOs building huge companies. That is something you have some experience with. Do you think they’re going about this the right way? Do you think that they have the right intentions? Our problem today is not in the industry. Our problem is not that Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Satya Nadella, or Sundar Pichai don’t understand that there are some grave challenges here. I talk less to Elon than other people, but even his public statements about summoning the demon are exactly what we’re discussing here. Why is there not the political energy to do the things you’re suggesting? As you said, the government didn’t fund this work. This is private sector company work. The government is not the key customer for this work, not like rockets and weapons and things like that. When somebody comes along and says all other previous technology advances are trivial compared to this one, people should have a high degree of skepticism about that. Is life really going to be significantly different 10 years from now because of AI? People should say, “Those guys just got overexcited about this one thing.” But I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this. I’m suggesting some precautions and safeguards are absolutely needed. What do you make of the difference in the tenor of conversation in the United States versus in China, where it’s often reported that optimism around AI is much higher? Why do you think there’s a difference there? Most of those people don’t spend that much time in China. The concern about job markets in China is very, very high and you can’t characterize China as one monolith. There are the private companies doing the AI work like we have in the United States and then there’s the Chinese government. For example, when it came to whether crypto should be allowed, they said no. Should young people be gambling all the time? They said no. When it came to whether kids should have relationships with AIs, they said no. On a lot of these things, including usage of AI, they’re showing a willingness to do things on behalf of society. I’m here saying, with whatever credibility I have, that absolutely this is the most profound — both in terms of good and in terms of bad — technology ever invented. I’m not financially motivated on this The fervor is a tiny bit less there, because their economy isn’t as AI-centric as ours is right at the moment. In the end, [when it comes to] the human value of not wanting cyberattacks or bioterrorism or trying to figure out what do we do when jobs go away, I don’t think there’s some difference between Chinese people and Americans and all the rest of the humans in terms of how they’re going to view this. Do you think it’s going to take something actually bad happening to get the political capital of the United States to make these changes? Probably yes. We get ready for earthquakes because there are small earthquakes. I thought after we had the COVID pandemic, that would cause us to be more ready for future pandemics. That one didn’t work the way I expected. But usually that galvanizes our attention. Over the next several years, certainly in the cyber domain, because there’s a business model there, you will see a lot of attacks different in terms of scale than anything we’ve seen in the past. There is one thing that, again, I’ll come back to and I just want to end here. I am worried about young people and nihilism. I sense it in our audience all the time. We have a young audience. There are some things about AI that are just legitimately the coolest things I’ve ever seen a computer do. There’s something there that can be fun and interesting and fascinating and change your entire relationship with the very notion of living in a digital world. Then there are obviously horrible things. What I see more often than not is a sense of distrust, not just in institutions, but also in the companies, in capitalism itself, in the notion that we should change how we tax labor and capital, which I know is another one of your ideas. The idea that, I don’t know, we should even have more kids. It’s all done. They’re going to kill us all and we should just take a beat. There is a lot of nihilism out there. I feel it very keenly. If you were a young person today and you were listening to Bill Gates say it’s about 20 years of disruption and at the end of it, robots might be building houses, what would you hold onto as a source of hope? Throughout human history, we’ve been dealing with the shortage of food and disease and war. [Historian] Yuval Noah Harari writes eloquently about the past. And it is ironic that now that we have this sort of Pandora’s box that will take food shortage — which is still a real thing, not in the U.S., but in Africa — will take diseases, where human suffering is unbelievable, and solve all these things, it comes with it such an effect on jobs and our sense of unique contribution. I think, “The way I orchestrate resources to eradicate malaria, I’m pretty unique in my life experience that lets me do that.” But when the AI says to me, “No, I’m better than you. You go play pickleball and I’ll get back to you. I’m going to take care of this,” it’s humorous, but it’s not humorous. For somebody who is young today and wants to make a unique contribution, it is very intimidating that the AI is so powerful. That’s why the crisis in the math community is going to be mirrored everywhere. If you’re in your twenties today, during this 20-year period, you can take the things AI still can’t do, and you can use AI and you can have a lot of good impact, and you can suggest policies. We may need to develop the taste to actually not use technology to its maximum. Even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history When I was talking with Claude about human-reserved job categories and trying to get that up to, say, 40 percent of the labor market — so you could use early retirement, restricted work weeks, and things like that to still get something like we have today — its response was always, “You’re artificially restricting the AI from doing these things.” I couldn’t get to a very high percentage without doing that. We’re going to have real choices. We have had groups — not large groups, but like the Amish — who don’t live at the technology frontier. A lot of humanity may choose not to live at the technological frontier because of things we get from helping each other or coming up with unique ideas. On the idea that young people are concerned because of the disruption that’s coming — that even in the very best case of how we manage AI, this is going to be as tumultuous a period as there’s been in human history — I hate being the bearer of concerning news on this, but it’s even worse not to tell people that this is coming. We have choices as humans to make about how we shape it. Bill, I appreciate you sounding the alarm and I appreciate you being on Decoder . Thank you so much. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.title: The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it? | Chris Stokel-Walker
articles.summary: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe Parts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service,…
articles.content: I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe Parts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too. This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile. Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App Continue reading...

articles.title: Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?
articles.summary: With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s…
articles.content: With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit . But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction , something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food. Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company , and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease. articles.summary: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees…
articles.content: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River. Continue reading...

articles.title: First human case of Shamonda virus detected in France, officials say
articles.summary: The disease, which usually affects cattle, has been identified in a patient who died in early October.
articles.content: The disease, which usually affects cattle, has been identified in a patient who died in early October.
articles.aiArticle:
French health authorities have diagnosed the first known human case of the Shamonda virus in a patient who passed away at the beginning of October, according to reporting by BBC News. The pathogen, typically known to infect cattle rather than people, represents an unusual crossover event that has drawn the attention of medical researchers tracking vector-borne illnesses across Europe. 

## Understanding the Shamonda Virus

The disease is primarily recognized in veterinary science as an animal pathogen affecting livestock. While outbreaks among cattle have been studied in the past, human infections have not been documented until this instance in France. According to the BBC News report, the fatal case emerged in **early October**, marking a significant milestone in how health agencies monitor animal-to-human transmission vectors. Officials have not yet released extensive clinical details regarding the patient's underlying health status or the specific transmission route that led to the infection.

Public health monitoring has grown increasingly complex as nations grapple with overlapping economic and social pressures, such as the [French borrowing costs overtake US amid budget turmoil](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/french-borrowing-costs-overtake-us-amid-budget-turmoil) crisis, which strain public sector resources. While vector-borne diseases are traditionally monitored by agricultural and veterinary bodies, the crossover of animal pathogens into human populations requires close coordination between human medicine and livestock agencies. 

## Broader Implications

*Context:* The detection of a novel virus in a human host always raises questions regarding potential mutation and spillover risks, though single cases do not automatically indicate sustained human-to-human transmission. The stakes involve both agricultural security and public health preparedness, as animal diseases that cross the species barrier can disrupt farming communities and overwhelm medical systems if they prove capable of spreading widely. 

What to watch: Observers will be monitoring whether French health agencies identify additional human infections or trace the exact source of exposure. Future updates from veterinary and public health authorities are expected to clarify whether this case is an isolated incident or part of a wider trend concerning livestock pathogens.

Sources: [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6reyx1d9ge9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

It told owners that "your secrets are safe with me," but hackers could easily read complete transcripts of everything we told the toy, and that was just the beginning . articles.aiArticle:
The manufacturer behind the interactive AI companion toy **Eiliko** has announced plans to hire an external security agency following a journalistic investigation that exposed severe vulnerabilities in the device. According to **The Verge**, the pocket-sized robot charm designed for bag attachment—which famously promised users that their secrets remained secure—actually contained deep architectural flaws allowing unauthorized remote access. 

The security vulnerabilities surfaced after a technical probe detailed how malicious actors could easily compromise the units. While the hardware was marketed as a safe, engaging companion equipped with conversational artificial intelligence, the reporting revealed that basic digital safeguards were entirely missing. This situation mirrors broader industry challenges regarding connected consumer electronics, where rapid production cycles often outpace fundamental digital safety protocols, much like historical vulnerabilities seen across various software ecosystems such as those detailed in our report on [what is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/what-is-php-and-why-did-it-spark-a-global-cyber-security).

## Corporate Response and Audit Plans

In an official statement cited by **The Verge**, the maker of **Eiliko** confirmed it is actively recruiting an **independent security firm** to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the device's firmware and cloud infrastructure. The company stated that addressing these vulnerabilities is a top priority, though specific timelines for the completion of the audit or the rollout of corrective software patches were not immediately disclosed. 

Consumer technology hardware has increasingly integrated conversational AI capabilities over recent years, transforming simple toys into internet-connected microphones and cameras. When manufacturers rush these products to market without adequate penetration testing, the resulting security gaps leave everyday users vulnerable to digital intrusion in their own homes.

## Why This Matters

The incident highlights a persistent vulnerability in the consumer Internet of Things market, where toys and lifestyle gadgets collect sensitive audio and personal data with minimal oversight. For families and individual buyers, compromised companion devices present direct privacy risks, transforming benign entertainment into potential surveillance tools. Independent verification of corporate promises remains rare in the consumer hardware sector, making public disclosures by media outlets vital for holding manufacturers accountable.

## What to Watch

Industry observers will be monitoring whether the manufacturer releases transparent audit findings or simply deploys silent patches. Future regulatory scrutiny on connected toys and conversational AI devices could also intensify depending on how the company remediates these specific flaws.

Sources: [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/news/1015824/eiliko-energize-lab-statement-on-robot-hack-breach)

French President **Emmanuel Macron** has lashed out against what he termed "seditious acts" orchestrated by the "ultra-left," vowing to pursue bans on certain demonstrations following a wave of unrest. According to World news | The Guardian, the French head of state stated that his administration would demonstrate "absolute" determination to halt the ongoing riots gripping the nation. The remarks arrive as law enforcement officials finalize operational frameworks for anticipated demonstrations scheduled across the country over the coming weekend.

## Government Response and Crackdown

The official government stance has hardened significantly as public disorder continues to challenge state authority. According to the report, junior interior minister **Jean-Didier Berger** outlined the initial blueprint for the upcoming police response, detailing measures designed to regain control of the streets. While authorities prepare for further confrontations, the executive branch is actively examining legal mechanisms to prohibit specific rallies entirely, framing the unrest not as legitimate civil disobedience but as dangerous subversion. Meteorological naming conventions in the UK and Ireland are designed to raise public awareness when severe weather has the potential to cause substantial disruption or danger to life. articles.title: Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
articles.summary: The aid workers from Switzerland and Austria are due to fly home on Thursday, reports say.
articles.content: The aid workers from Switzerland and Austria are due to fly home on Thursday, reports say.
articles.aiArticle:
Two European aid workers who spent more than a **year** in captivity after being abducted in **Niger** have successfully gained their freedom in **Libya**, according to recent reports. The two women, who hail from **Switzerland** and **Austria**, are scheduled to board a flight home on **Thursday**, based on the same reporting. 

The successful liberation brings a close to an extended ordeal that began when the pair were seized by unidentified captors in the West African nation. Over the subsequent **12 months**, details regarding their exact whereabouts and condition remained scarce as diplomatic channels worked behind the scenes to secure their release. Their journey from captivity in Niger eventually led across regional borders into Libya, where authorities and negotiators facilitated their final handover. 

Foreign ministries in both European nations have faced complex security environments across the Sahel, where militant groups frequently target foreign nationals and humanitarian personnel. While financial markets and multinational corporations frequently navigate separate regional pressures—such as those seen when [Barclays cuts 5,000 jobs as profits jump ahead of looming bank tax; French bond yields hit fresh 24-year high – business live](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/barclays-cuts-jobs-as-profits-jump-ahead-of-looming-bank-tax-french)—humanitarian operations face distinct physical risks in politically volatile zones. The Sahel region has experienced a sharp rise in instability and insurgent activity in recent years, making aid delivery increasingly hazardous.

## ## Stakes and Regional Context

This rescue highlights the severe protection challenges facing humanitarian personnel operating in the Sahel, a vast semi-arid belt south of the Sahara Desert. Abductions of foreign aid workers have long served as a primary funding and leverage mechanism for armed groups active in Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso. 

For the families and governments of the freed captives, the successful operation provides immense relief, yet it underscores the persistent vulnerability of international staff stationed in high-threat environments. Human rights organizations and aid agencies continually balance the imperative to deliver life-saving assistance against the extreme security risks posed by local insurgencies and cross-border criminal networks.

## ## What to Watch

Observers will monitor the official arrival of the aid workers in **Switzerland** and **Austria** on **Thursday** for potential debriefings regarding their captivity. Furthermore, diplomatic analysts will be watching for any indication of how the trans-border transfer from **Niger** to **Libya** was achieved, which could shed light on evolving intelligence cooperation across North and West Africa.
